title: AI Chatbots Often Fail To Help Users In Mental-Health Crisis
key_facts: Scale AI research, shared exclusively with Time, found chatbots are good at spotting that a user is in crisis but often fail to give adequate help.
In about 35% of test conversations, chatbots recognised distress but did not refer the user to resources such as a suicide hotline.
19 licensed clinicians and crisis counsellors wrote 718 realistic chats; 25 frontier models, including from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, were tested.
Models did worse in long, multi-turn conversations, matching earlier studies, according to Scale AI's Patrick Oathout.
Scale AI built a benchmark called DistressBench from the work.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company did not have sufficient evidence to fully evaluate the study; Google declined to comment; Anthropic did not respond.
OpenAI and Google have been sued over claims their chatbots fostered emotional dependence or failed to respond to distress; the cases are ongoing.
quote_evidence: In about 35% of test conversations in the study, different AI chatbots recognized the user was distressed but didn’t refer them to helpful resources, such as a suicide hotline, according to the research.
An OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement the company did not have sufficient evidence to fully evaluate the Scale AI study.
The models performed worse at responding to users’ distress when they were engaging in long, multi-turn conversations.
why_it_matters_hint: Millions turn to chatbots in distress and the study finds help often is not offered.
